text:
that's the biggest question for me. it's a $50 price difference between them where I'm at, with the Arc being cheaper.

I'll say that the performance from the Arc appears to be more consistent based on different tests I've seen. B580 also has more VRAM, which can make a big difference on certain games.

I think 5060's DLSS is supported by more games, while the B850's XeSS isn't as much (not completely sure, just what I'm thinking from a cursory glance). Additionally, both DLSS and XeSS are only supported by certain games; a couple of the games that I want to play at 1440p with mods, Skyrim and Fallout 4, aren't supported in DLSS or XeSS, so I'd be relying on raw power from both cards. but if you're focusing on current or newer games, this shouldn't be an issue.

I'm also guessing that the 5060 does better ray tracing than the B580, though I haven't seen these cards put head-to-head in that area.

in my case, I believe the VRAM will probably go a longer ways, so the B580 is likely better for me.

text:
It's the same as if I took a GTX 1060 and paired it with a twoyear older i5 4460, then complained about having a GPU problem. On top of that, you don’t even have a ReBAR feature, but just plain PCIe. That means the moment you lack Resizable BAR, the CPU has to access multiple memory blocks separately, which creates an additional bottleneck.
Hardware Unboxed actually made a video about this, but they didn’t fully explain or clarify the issue. They just briefly said the GPU has a problem, but in reality, it’s not just the GPU. I agree that it requires more processed data to prepare frames, but that’s exactly because of those multiple memory blocks and a different kind of access handled by the CPU rather than the GPU.
However, this is a feature in itself that actually boosts the graphics chip’s performance.
That said, I disagree with the idea that the GPU should be paired with an older AMD CPU and used primarily for 1080p. The GPU is a pretty solid chip, capable of pushing 1440p easily even paired with an i5 12400f without any issues. Personally, I have an i5 12400F and use an Arc B580 setup occasionally for light gaming. I also have another rig with an AMD 7800X3D, which is a slightly older high end CPU paired with an RX 7900 XTX, and that combo performs well for job.
But the Arc B580 doesn’t make sense to pair with older CPUs that’s exactly why. Imagine pairing a GTX 1060 with an i5 4460 or an RX 5700 XT with an i5 8400 it just wouldn’t make sense because of PCIe version limitations, right?

author: @AlbinoAlagoano

text: @AlbinoAlagoano It performs well because the CPU isn’t that old, and he made a great comparison. Also, the system doesn’t use ReBAR, it uses SAM which is AMD’s version of the same concept. Both ReBAR and SAM allow the CPU to access the full GPU memory instead of being limited to 256MB chunks. However, SAM is specifically optimized for AMD CPUs and GPUs working together, which can result in slightly better efficiency or compatibility if you have AMD card not Intel. With AMD platforms, SAM is more tightly integrated at the firmware and driver level, so it may behave a bit differently compared to how ReBAR works on Intel or mixed setups.
author: @edwardbenchmarks

text:
@edwardbenchmarks  SAM is exclusive to systems with AMD GPUs and CPUs.
When using an NVIDIA or Intel GPU, it uses ReBAR.
SAM is simply an optimized REBAR with drivers, so it works on full AMD systems.
That is, the 5600 supports REBAR and PCIE 4.0 (it also depends on the motherboard). When using the ARC B580, it uses REBAR, not SAM.

text:
I have an Arc B580 paired with an i5 12400F, and it works perfectly no problems at all. The GPU is always running at 100%. There is no driver overhead, that’s just nonsense and misinformation and instead of someone explaining it, everyone is just talking about driver overhead. Reason it uses more CPU cores than other GPUs is because the CPU can access the entire GPU framebuffer memory at once, instead of being limited to 256MB chunks.
Older CPU can’t do this because ReBAR isn’t fully optimized for them, or they simply use the basic AMD implementation, which makes a difference. Generally speaking, the i5 12400F is a mid CPU that’s two years older than the GPU, is completely reasonable and normal.
Arc B580 isn’t meant just for 1080p. In fact, 1080p can be a challenge because it requires processing more data the GPU itself is capable of rendering higher frame rates, so it needs more data fed to it.
It’s like if I took an RTX 5060 and paired it with an i5 10400F, then complained that it can’t handle 1080p. The RTX 5060 requires just as much data as the Arc B580 and demands more processed frames from the CPU. It’s basically the same situation.
Similarly in past, you couldn’t pair an RX 5600 XT with an i5 8400 without running into issues due to PCIe version and feature limitations and the same applies here. If you don’t have a proper ReBAR compatible CPU, don’t buy it.
If you don’t have at least an i5 12400F, I don’t see the point in buying the Arc B580, which costs twice as much as that CPU. I paid $120 new for mine, seriously.
